title: Sticky note: domestic R2R bonding films for HBM stacking
idea: Random stimulus 'sticky note' -> stick, peel, restick. US roll-to-roll coating lines produce temporary bond/debond tapes and non-conductive bonding films (NCF) for thin-wafer HBM stacking, now sourced from a few Japanese suppliers.
why: Removes a single-region chokepoint in HBM back-end; tape supply scales with coater lines in months, not fab years.

title: Temporary tattoo: micro-transfer-print DRAM chiplets directly onto accelerator BEOL
idea: Random stimulus 'temporary tattoo' -> press, peel, transfer. Elastomer stamps pick up ~10,000 thinned 100 um DRAM chiplets per stroke from source wafers made in many small fabs and print them onto accelerator BEOL or panels, with printed RDL.
why: Near-memory without an interposer or TSV stack; lets small mature fabs feed AI memory, and assembly capex per bit drops sharply.

title: Back to polycide: tungsten-free legacy-node memory flow
idea: Polycide (WSi, CoSi2) wordlines were abandoned for tungsten because their resistance scaled badly in narrow lines, which now ties DRAM to tungsten (China ~80%). At 180 nm and above that problem does not exist: run legacy-node memory and companion chips with poly/CoSi2 wordlines, Al-Cu interconnect and Ti/TiN-lined Al-reflow plugs (a 1990s technique) instead of W plugs.
why: Scarce resources: removes tungsten from the old-node memory and companion-chip flow, shielding that supply from a single-country chokepoint.

title: Carbide-tool zinc reclaim feeds domestic tungsten targets and WF6
idea: Machine shops recycle cemented-carbide tools by the zinc process. Build a U.S. stream that turns scrap carbide and spent tungsten targets into 6N WF6 precursor and sputter targets: zinc-melt breakdown, oxidation, APT conversion, then fluorination or pressing.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): domestic secondary tungsten could cover all DRAM wordline and contact demand from scrap.

title: Kit fab: shipyard-built cleanroom modules on pre-permitted pads
idea: Ideal: a fab built in a week. Closest achievable: standardized cleanroom and sub-fab modules with pre-integrated AMHS, utilities and exhaust are built in shipyards, barged in and bolted onto pre-permitted pads.
why: Capital and time: construction drops from ~3 years to ~14 months, with 20-30% lower construction capex.

title: US Memories reborn: take-or-pay consortium with escrowed exit penalties
idea: US Memories (1989; IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed before breaking ground because members walked away when DRAM prices fell. Fix exactly that: members sign 10-year take-or-pay offtake contracts for capacity units (wafer starts per month) with a price collar, and post exit penalties equal to their share of unrecovered capex into escrow, so a price dip cannot dissolve the fab.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: pre-selling ~60-70% of output cuts the cost of capital for a $15B+ fab by several points and keeps a U.S. DRAM fab financeable through a downturn.

title: Heme-inspired spin-crossover molecular memory printed onto CMOS
idea: Hemoglobin's iron flips between high-spin and low-spin states when oxygen binds. Fe(II) spin-crossover complexes designed for room-temperature bistability and electric-field switching are printed or vapor-deposited over CMOS sense transistors, which read the spin state as a change in channel conductance.
why: Moves supply to chemical synthesis rather than fab tools; molecular-scale bits with no capacitor.

title: Strategic DRAM Reserve of nitrogen-vaulted known-good-die wafers
idea: Ideal: a shortage that never reaches users. Closest achievable: the government buys tested DRAM wafers during gluts, stores them diced on tape in dry-nitrogen vaults (unpowered die keep for decades), and releases them to OSATs for packaging whenever contract prices pass a trigger.
why: Price spikes and pig cycle: a 60-90 day bit buffer could cap 4x spikes, and smoother prices lower the cost of capital for all fabs.

title: Mycorrhizal memory commons: cross-tenant DRAM lending over CXL fabric
idea: Like fungal networks shuttling carbon from sun-rich trees to shaded ones, rack-scale CXL 3.x switches let servers with idle DRAM lend pages to memory-starved neighbours. A broker reads per-host free-memory telemetry, rebalances continuously, and pays lenders per GB-hour from a 'carbon credit' ledger.
why: Clouds strand ~20-30% of installed DRAM; recovering half of it raises usable supply ~10-15% with zero new wafers (supply, cost per bit).

title: 1 Gb UCIe DRAM tiles so many small fabs feed one package
idea: Scale jump from die to package: define a tiny standard DRAM chiplet (1 Gb, UCIe-like edge interface, fixed footprint). Small or legacy fabs anywhere make tiles, and packaging houses tile dozens of them, possibly from different makers, onto a base die.
why: Small dies yield far better (yield falls exponentially with area) and let sub-scale fabs contribute bits. Creates a distributed supply base instead of three vendors.

title: Pharma-style CDMO for fabless DRAM cell designers
idea: Adapted from biologics CDMOs like Lonza: a memory CDMO offers a qualified DRAM front end (capacitor module, buried wordline, periphery transistors) on which fabless memory startups tape out their own array and cell designs under tech-transfer contracts and pay per wafer.
why: Separates memory innovation from owning a $15B fab and does for memory what TSMC did for logic; cuts an entrant's capital need ~100x and widens the supplier base (capital intensity).

title: Hydrocarbon immersion cold racks rescue retention-marginal recycled DIMMs
idea: Fuse fluorine-free synthetic hydrocarbon (PAO) immersion cooling with second-life memory. Recycled modules that fail 85 °C retention run at about 30 °C, where leakage drops roughly 10× and refresh intervals stretch, which re-qualifies rejected parts.
why: Expands the reusable pool of old DRAM by an estimated 20-40% and cuts refresh energy, avoiding the fluorinated two-phase coolants under PFAS restriction.

title: Hotel concierge: on-module DRAM front desk over flash storage
idea: A concierge keeps tonight's keys at the desk and everything else in storage. An on-module 'memory hotel' pairs 16 GB of DRAM with 256 GB of low-latency SLC flash behind a controller that predicts and prefetches hot 4 KB pages, presenting 272 GB to the host as byte-addressable CXL memory.
why: Meets the 10x constraint in capacity per module: ~10x for about the same module cost, since SLC flash is ~1/10 of DRAM's $/bit. A hot-set hit rate above 99% keeps average latency DRAM-class, but misses cost ~5-10 us and flash endurance limits write-heavy use.

title: Vertical nanographite contacts replace tungsten and cobalt plugs
idea: In narrow plugs, metal resistivity is dominated by surface and grain-boundary scattering plus barrier volume, while vertically oriented graphene sheets conduct in-plane along the plug with no barrier. Grow carbon nanowall contacts by catalyst-free ~400 C PECVD inside contact holes and dope them by FeCl3 intercalation (Fe, Cl, C only).
why: Scarce resource: removes W and Co from bitline and storage-node contacts using limitless, domestic carbon; contact resistance at the TiN interface is the main risk.

title: 48-hour printed test sockets for orphan salvaged packages
idea: Formula 1 teams iterate parts overnight. A 10-person shop uses high-resolution resin and two-photon printing plus pogo pins to make a BGA test socket for any orphan DRAM package in 48 hours instead of 8-12 weeks, so refurbishers can test whatever arrives.
why: Removes a hidden bottleneck in the reuse and micro-fab supply chains.

title: Eliminate the cleanroom building: sealed-pod minimal fabs in warehouses
idea: Eliminate the ballroom cleanroom: adopt the minimal-fab model (half-inch wafers in sealed shuttles, shoebox tools with local mini-environments) to make radiation-hard, automotive and defense DRAM in ordinary industrial buildings.
why: Line capex falls from billions to ~$10-50M for low-volume, high-value memory; slashes water and HVAC energy; onshores defense memory.

title: Pioneer-species beachhead: enter at 125 C niche, scale downward
idea: Like lichens colonizing fresh lava where nothing else grows, a U.S. startup memory maker launches only in 125-150 C automotive, defense and downhole markets that incumbents underserve, where premiums are 3-5x per bit, and uses that learning curve to scale into commodity later.
why: Funds a domestic manufacturing learning curve with high margins instead of fighting a price war in commodity DRAM.

title: Goto's Parametron Revived as Resonant Charge-Recovery DRAM Wordline Drivers
idea: Revive Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron (resonant LC circuits that ran Japan's PC-1 computer) as on-package inductor tanks that swing DRAM wordlines and bitline groups sinusoidally over a ~10 ns window and return their charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground, recovering 80-90% of CV2.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): CV2 on ~3 V wordlines and ~1 V bitlines dominates array energy; adiabatic recovery gives ~5-10x lower array energy per access; a periphery-only change licensable to every existing DRAM fab.

title: Polar explorer's 77 K cold-memory pods run by gas suppliers
idea: A polar explorer knows cold preserves things. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by more than 10^6, so a cell needs ~0.3 fF instead of 5 fF: the 70:1 pillar gives way to a planar MIM cap over a vertical-channel 4F^2 transistor, and 7 such tiers are bonded. The pods are LN2-immersion memory, sold as a service by industrial-gas firms.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 vs 6F^2 (1.5x) times 7 tiers is ~10x bits/mm^2. Deleting the high-aspect-ratio capacitor module and refresh offsets the bonding and cooling cost; cryo-CMOS sensing margins are the risk.

title: Digital-twin DRAM fab flight school for process engineers
idea: Ideal: experienced fab engineers available instantly. Closest achievable: a national academy runs a full-fab simulator that replays real, anonymized excursion data from partners and certifies yield engineers in 6 months, the way pilots train on simulators.
why: Talent bottleneck for U.S. fabs: roughly halves the learning curve of a ramp.

title: Minify cycle risk with exchange-traded DRAM bit futures
idea: List standardized DRAM futures (per Gb-month, DDR5 and HBM contracts, physically settled at bonded warehouses) so fabs hedge future output and buyers hedge spikes.
why: Price risk drives underinvestment and 4x swings; hedging lowers fabs' risk premium and enables counter-cyclical capex.

title: Ocean Spray-style buyer cooperative owning a DRAM fab
idea: Adapted from agricultural cooperatives: PC, phone, auto and server OEMs buy co-op shares in a jointly owned fab. Each member gets wafer allocation in proportion to equity, pays cost-plus, and gets surplus back as patronage dividends.
why: Guarantees members supply through shortages and strips out the oligopoly margin (~30-60% at peak), lowering effective cost per bit (cost, supply security).

title: Campus-scale HBM stack-and-test micro-lines inside datacenter parks
idea: Scale jump from the global back-end supply chain to the campus: put small TSV-stacking, hybrid-bonding and test lines inside datacenter campuses, so known-good DRAM wafers arrive and finished HBM goes straight to accelerator boards on site.
why: HBM back-end capacity and a 20-30% yield loss are bottlenecks. Local lines add capacity, cut weeks of logistics, and let failed stacks be reworked instead of scrapped.

title: Minify the litho tool to a spin coater: block-copolymer arrays
idea: Spin-coat high-chi block copolymers that phase-separate into 12-16 nm pitch hexagonal dot arrays, use them as etch masks for vertical pillar cells, align domains to wordlines with coarse i-line trenches (graphoepitaxy), and absorb assembly defects with redundancy.
why: Coater + bake plate + i-line stepper instead of EUV gives ~20x lower capex per wafer, and sub-15 nm pitch packs ~4x more cells than 6F2 at F=12 nm: ~80-100x lower cost per GB.

title: Magnetic-seeded sedimentation recovers rare-earth ceria CMP slurry
idea: Ceria abrasive is co-precipitated around superparamagnetic Fe3O4 seeds; spent slurry passes high-gradient magnetic separators that recapture the abrasive, then Stokes-settling classification restores the size distribution for reuse.
why: Cuts ceria (China-dominated rare earth) purchases ~60-80% and slurry waste.

title: Socketed-memory mandate so laptop and server RAM can be harvested
idea: Inverts 'memory is soldered for life': require CAMM/DIMM-style sockets in laptops and servers above a size threshold, plus a standard test interface, so modules can be removed, retested and redeployed at end of device life.
why: Reuse/recycling: soldered LPDDR is shredded today; making it harvestable could feed a second-life stream of several percent of annual bits.

title: Carbon credits for avoided NF3, SF6 and CF4 finance fab capex
idea: Fuse a fluorine-free DRAM flow with verified carbon-credit issuance. Avoided F-gases (NF3 GWP about 16,100, SF6 about 23,500, CF4 about 7,400) earn credits over a baseline fab's emissions, which are pre-sold as offtake to fund construction.
why: A typical fab emits about 0.5-1 Mt CO2e per year in F-gases. Credits could fund 5-10% of capex and lower $/bit.

title: Complementary Cu2O/ZnO oxide periphery lets entire memory live in BEOL
idea: Periphery (~49% of the die) is what pins memory to single-crystal silicon. Pair p-type Cu2O and n-type Zn-Si-O TFTs into low-temperature CMOS sense amps and decoders so both array and periphery deposit at <=400 C, allowing 10+ complete memory layers on any substrate.
why: Density and capital: monolithic 3D memory without 26-tier lateral Si transistors; the risk is Cu2O hole mobility (~1-5 cm^2/V-s) limiting periphery speed.

title: Split-fab: periphery on legacy partner wafers, arrays on DRAM wafers
idea: Box[Integration=wafer-to-wafer hybrid bond x Fab=array-only DRAM wafer + periphery on depreciated 28-40 nm logic fab x Owner=two-company tolling x Scale=distributed]: the DRAM fab patterns only cells, and partner logic fabs (including U.S. 300 mm legacy lines) make sense amps, decoders and I/O that are bonded face-to-face.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die; moving it off DRAM wafers frees ~40% more leading-edge DRAM wafer area for bits and moves value to U.S. legacy fabs.

title: Preliminary anti-action: cold-crucible levitation Czochralski removes quartz crucible dependency
idea: TRIZ #9 Preliminary anti-action: pre-empt the Spruce Pine chokepoint by growing DRAM-grade silicon in water-cooled segmented copper cold crucibles with induction-levitated melt (skull melting), so the melt never touches high-purity quartz.
why: Scarce-resource intensity: removes >80% single-source HPQ crucible exposure and also cuts oxygen contamination.

title: Patchwork-quilt modules stitched from partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Quilters make full blankets from remnants. Dies that fail full spec because of a few dead banks or subarrays are scrapped or sold as junk today; instead, mount them on an organic substrate. A small 'quilting' controller holds each die's bad-region map and presents one contiguous address space by interleaving across the surviving banks.
why: Cost per bit and yield: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output that is lost today. That is like getting a free mini-fab per large fab with no new capex.

title: Catalytic-converter-style tungsten recovery from CVD exhaust and targets
idea: Like recovering platinum metals from scrapped catalysts, fab abatement adds cold traps that capture unreacted WF6 and W-bearing chamber deposits, which a regional refiner converts back to WF6 or APT together with spent sputter targets.
why: Cuts virgin tungsten demand 30-50%, reducing exposure to the ~80% China concentration.

title: Substitute single-crystal wafers with crucible-free amorphous carrier substrates
idea: Because <=400 C memory tiers need no crystalline silicon, swap prime CZ wafers for reclaimed test wafers or glass carriers that hold only memory tiers, later bonded to a small periphery die.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine crucible and prime-wafer dependence from most of the memory area; substrate cost per wafer drops ~5-10x.

title: Eliminate dummy monitor wafers with in-situ virtual metrology
idea: Eliminate the monitor, dummy and seasoning wafers that eat wafer starts: in-chamber optical emission and RF sensors plus virtual metrology qualify tools on product wafers, keeping reclaimed monitors only for audits.
why: Frees ~5-10% of fab wafer capacity and the matching substrate and crucible demand.

title: Cheap substitute: panel-level DRAM on idle display-glass TFT lines
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap objects: replace costly silicon wafers with 5.5 m^2 Gen-8.5 glass panels from idle display fabs, using the standard oxide-TFT backplane flow plus one added mask for a high-k storage capacitor, to make bulk low-speed capacity-tier DRAM.
why: Cost and capital: ~tens of GB per panel on fully depreciated lines; trades density for vast idle area.

title: Pure-play DRAM array foundry for fabless memory designers
idea: Box[Owner=foundry x Medium=standard 1T1C array PDK x Integration=customer periphery/logic x Business=wafer-per-month service]: a DRAM fab sells array wafers with a PDK and IP library, the way TSMC sells logic, so fabless firms design custom DRAMs (AI, automotive, CXL) without owning a fab.
why: Industry structure: opens DRAM to many designers, raising fab utilization and innovation; could support new entrants with zero capex.

title: DRAM-only 450 mm fab reviving immersion 450 prototypes
idea: Po: the wafer is twice as big. The 450 mm transition stalled partly because EUV never had a 450 mm version; a DUV-only DRAM fab revives the 450 mm immersion scanner and process-tool prototypes from the G450C era and runs DRAM wafers with 2.25x the area per wafer pass.
why: Past estimates promised ~20-30% lower cost per die at 450 mm; DRAM's single-product volume justifies a dedicated tool set; attacks cost per bit and capital per bit.

title: Quilter uses whole cloth: undiced wafer-scale memory cassettes
idea: A quilter works with whole cloth. Skip dicing, packaging and DIMM PCBs: ship whole 300 mm DRAM wafers with wafer-level redundancy routing and edge contacts, stacked 20 deep in a liquid-cooled cassette that plugs into a rack CXL switch.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: one wafer holds ~1.5-2 TB, so a 20-wafer cassette is ~35 TB in ~4 L, versus hundreds of liters of server DIMM slots. Packaging, PCB and per-die test savings (~15-20% of module cost) pay for the redundancy.

title: Borrow solar photoluminescence imaging tools for cheap substrate screening
idea: The solar industry maps wafers with band-to-band photoluminescence cameras in under a second per wafer on <$500k tools. Adapt them to map lifetime-killing defects and metal contamination in incoming DRAM substrates and after key thermal steps.
why: Cuts metrology capital for micro-fabs, where $10-50M inspection tools are a barrier.

title: Substitute integrated memory makers with a pure-play DRAM foundry
idea: Swap the three vertically integrated DRAM makers for a TSMC-style pure-play DRAM foundry offering a cell-array process plus design kits, so fabless memory companies and hyperscalers tape out custom DRAM.
why: Opens DRAM to new entrants and custom parts, spreading fab capital over many customers and raising utilization through cycles.

title: Magnify self-ordering: anodized-alumina pore forests replace array lithography
idea: Anodize aluminum films so they self-organize ~10^10 nanopores/cm2 in an electrochemical bath, register the pores to the wordline grid with a nanoimprinted dimple pattern, and ALD-fill each pore as a vertical capacitor plus oxide-semiconductor channel; repeat for 3-4 tiers.
why: Swaps 5-7 EUV array layers (and their depreciation burden) for a ~$10k bath at near-DRAM density per tier; stacking tiers in a small fab targets ~100x lower cost per GB.

title: Lehi fab lesson: swing fab toggling new memory and DRAM
idea: 3D XPoint's dedicated Lehi fab ran far below capacity, and its fixed cost helped kill Optane. Fix: launch any new memory in a swing fab whose toolset is ~80% shared with a DRAM flow, with a dual-qualified recipe library, so wafer starts move between DRAM and the new memory each quarter as demand changes.
why: Capital intensity: a new memory rides DRAM's utilization (keeping the fab ~85%+ loaded) instead of carrying an empty fab, and in shortages the same tools make DRAM.

title: Memory outlives compute: debondable HBM stacks
idea: Reverse the lifetime hierarchy: HBM stacks attach to the interposer with low-temperature reversible solder or thermoplastic bonds. When the GPU retires, the stacks are lifted off and remounted on new base packages for inference or CXL use.
why: HBM wafers carry the TSV tax (3x area per bit). Second-life stacks use essentially no fab water (>10x cut on that supply), and fewer new HBM wafers are needed per year of service.

title: Epigenetic-mark 1T charge-trap DRAM produced in NOR flash fabs
idea: Methyl marks change gene expression without changing the gene. A 1-transistor cell with a ~2 nm tunnel oxide and a nitride trap layer stores bits as threshold shifts that last seconds to minutes, written by fast direct tunneling, in NOR and embedded-flash fabs that already run charge-trap modules.
why: Repurposes declining NOR capacity; 1T density without a capacitor and refresh intervals ~1000x longer.

title: Harvest wafer-edge die normally lost to nonuniformity
idea: Inverts 'edge die are scrap': shrink edge exclusion and keep the outer ring of die, whose CD and film-thickness drift raises cell faults up to the 1% budget, and sell them in the error-tolerant grade.
why: Die per wafer: adds roughly 3-6% sellable die per 300 mm wafer with no extra process.

title: Sanitize-not-shred policy saves decommissioned DIMMs
idea: Box[Policy=NIST 800-88 style guidance that certifies power-off plus pattern overwrite for volatile DRAM x Owner=standards body + insurers x Channel=reuse market]: since DRAM is volatile, verified pattern-write and power-off clears it, so certify that and stop the security-driven shredding of retired server memory.
why: Unlocks the reuse supply that pre-owned and repair models need; potentially tens of millions of DIMMs per year.

title: Monk's vow of simplicity: RAM-Star label for lean software
idea: Take a monk's austerity: federal procurement adopts a 'RAM Star' certification, modeled on Energy Star, that requires software to meet memory-footprint benchmarks per workload (browsers, Java services, containers), backed by runtime guidance (compressed pointers, arena allocators, page sharing).
why: Demand reduction: software bloat drives DRAM per device; a 20-30% footprint cut across federal and enterprise fleets frees exabyte-scale supply at no fab cost.

title: Vertical farmer grows 64 crystal tiers in one epitaxy season
idea: A vertical farmer grows many layers in one season instead of buying more land. One epitaxy run deposits 64 Si/SiGe pairs; a single slit mask lets the SiGe be removed selectively, freeing 64 single-crystal Si channel tiers that are wrapped in ALD gates, with lateral ZrO2 capacitors in the space the SiGe left. U.S. epi-tool makers and a DRAM startup co-own the flow.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density each gives ~12x bits/mm^2. The tiers come from one epi run and one etch rather than 64 litho cycles, so wafer cost stays near a planar DRAM wafer's.

title: Ballroom-free fab: mini-environments end cleanroom humidification
idea: Rearrange cleanliness from the room to the wafer: wafers live only in nitrogen-purged FOUPs and sealed tool mini-environments, and the building around them runs as ordinary grey space. That removes most make-up air humidification and the cooling-tower load for HVAC.
why: Shrinking the controlled air volume ~10-50x cuts HVAC humidification and cooling water ~10x and lowers fab shell capex.

title: Shipyard-built floating DRAM fab towed to a U.S. port
idea: Inverts 'fabs are built on site over 3-5 years': cleanroom, subfab and utility decks are fabricated in parallel in a shipyard on a ballasted concrete caisson, towed to a deep-water U.S. port and grounded on the seabed for vibration stability, then hooked to grid and desalinated water.
why: Capital time and U.S. manufacturability: moves construction to idle shipyard labor and parallel prefab, targeting ~18-24 months to first wafer instead of 3-5 years.

title: High-bandwidth flash plus SRAM appliances replacing DRAM for weights
idea: Worse: keep entire models resident in DRAM because flash is 'too slow'. Flip: stack many-plane NAND on a logic die for high-bandwidth parallel reads and prefetch weight tiles into on-die SRAM ahead of the layer schedule, so the only memories are static SRAM and NAND that retains data unpowered.
why: Zero refresh, and the bulk store comes from abundant NAND at ~5-10x lower cost per bit.

title: Eliminate forced DDR5 migration: new DDR4 boards for dual-support CPUs
idea: Eliminate the platform change that strands DDR4: contract an ODM to build new DDR4 boards for CPUs and embedded SoCs whose controllers support both DDR4 and DDR5, aimed at the reclaimed-DDR4 pool; ~$800k NRE and first batch.
why: Gives used DDR4 a large new home and moves buyers off scarce DDR5.

title: HBM speed-bin rejects repurposed into edge inference cards
idea: Combine HBM stacks that fail top speed or thermal bins with lower-clock edge and enterprise inference accelerators designed around derated HBM, sold as a 'B-grade HBM' SKU class.
why: HBM yields are down 20-30%, so monetizing near-miss stacks recovers costly TSV wafer area and effectively raises HBM output 5-15%.

title: Consortium defect-map commons that pools years of yield learning
idea: Time compression by pooling: member fabs upload anonymized, federated defect and wafer-map data, and shared models flag excursions that one fab alone would need years of wafers to recognize.
why: Yield ramp time is cost. Cutting a new node's ramp by ~6-9 months raises cumulative bit output 10-15%.

title: Tesla gigacasting adapted: wafer-scale DRAM slabs skip packaging entirely
idea: Adapted from gigacasting, where one casting replaces ~70 stamped parts: keep each 300 mm DRAM wafer whole as a ~1 TB memory slab with on-wafer redundancy routing, and mount it on a U.S.-made glass or silicon backplane with bonded CXL controllers, skipping dicing, packaging and offshore OSAT steps.
why: Removes the Asian packaging/test dependence, recovers scribe area (~5-8%) and gives TB-class pooled-memory appliances made entirely in the U.S. (U.S. manufacturability, cost per bit).

title: Substitute new bits with negabytes bought through memory demand response
idea: Swap adding supply for paying data centers to free memory, as utilities pay for negawatts: an exchange pays per freed GB-month verified by telemetry (compression, dedupe, tiering), and the freed modules return to market.
why: Creates virtual supply from the ~30-50% of server DRAM that is stranded or idle, potentially adding the equivalent of a fab's output with zero capex.

title: Moire-fringe alignment upgrades refurbished ArF steppers to DRAM overlay
idea: Dual-grating alignment marks produce a Moire beat that magnifies nm misalignment into um fringes read by a retrofit camera, feeding a piezo fine stage. That lets secondhand 2000s-era ArF steppers reach ~2-3 nm overlay for array layers.
why: Refurbished tools cost 5-10% of new, expanding litho capacity for new entrants.

title: Magnify HBM life: debond retired stacks and remount them
idea: Laser-release and thermally debond HBM stacks from retired AI accelerators, re-bump them, and mount them on fresh low-cost silicon or glass interposers for inference cards binned at lower bandwidth.
why: HBM pays a ~3x wafer-area-per-bit TSV tax up front; a second life amortizes that tax, roughly halving effective wafer area per HBM-bit-year.

title: Hydrogen-blistered donor wafers reused tenfold, device layers re-transferable
idea: Build the DRAM array in a Smart-Cut layer: implanted hydrogen forms a blistering plane that splits a thin Si film onto a carrier with a laser-release oxide. The donor is CMP-reclaimed ~10x, and at end of life the device layer lifts off so carrier and silicon are reclaimed.
why: Cuts Cz wafer and HPQ crucible consumption up to ~10x and closes the substrate loop.

title: Inference model cartridges in via-programmed mask ROM
idea: Worse: hold frozen model weights in refreshing DRAM. Flip: ship weights of stable production models as via-programmed ROM cartridges built on 28-40 nm lines, one custom via mask per model, with 20-50 ns random reads.
why: Read-only weights need zero refresh; dense ROM cells on mature nodes free DRAM for truly dynamic data.

title: Skipping: open shared qualification lab cutting new-entrant DRAM qualification to months
idea: TRIZ #21 Rushing through: a neutral lab runs one public, JEDEC-plus qualification suite (retention, row hammer, burn-in, platform interop) whose results all major CPU/GPU vendors accept, so new suppliers skip 12-18 months of per-customer qualification.
why: Market entry barrier: lets new fabs' bits reach servers ~1 year sooner.

title: Piezo acoustic-emission sensors predict solder fatigue before memory fails
idea: An AlN thin-film piezo sensor on the module substrate hears acoustic-emission bursts from solder microcracks and delamination, and a counter in SPD flags the module for re-ball or repair before hard failure.
why: Turns catastrophic failures into scheduled repairs, keeping modules in service and reusable.

title: No silicon, no litho: self-ordered anodic alumina capacitor templates
idea: Forced limit: no wafer and no capacitor lithography. Aluminium foil from electrolytic-capacitor plants is anodized into self-ordered nanopores (AR 100+), lined by ALD with high-k and electrodes as storage capacitors, then bonded to TFT access arrays.
why: Capacitor charge wall: AR beyond 115 with no lithography or EUV; reuses the capacitor-foil industry.

title: Elpida's yen-and-cycle death: a cleared DRAM bit futures market
idea: Elpida failed in 2012 with competitive technology, killed by a strong yen and a price cycle it could not hedge. Fix: a cleared futures and options exchange on a standard contract (e.g. 1 Tb of DDR5-equivalent per quarter, cash-settled against a published contract-price index) lets makers sell forward and buyers lock in supply, as airlines hedge jet fuel.
why: Capital intensity: hedgeable revenue could cut memory makers' risk premium by ~2-3 points of WACC, worth ~$300-450M a year on a $15B fab, and buyers' forward commitments fund new capacity earlier.

title: Eliminate overprovisioning: working-set audit with shared-savings DIMM resale
idea: Eliminate padded memory configs: a startup deploys eBPF working-set profilers across a customer's fleet for 60 days, proves which DIMMs are never touched, pulls them, and resells them, splitting proceeds; $1M funds tooling plus five enterprise pilots.
why: Enterprise servers often touch only 40-60% of installed DRAM; freeing 20% at 4x prices pays customers and adds supply at once.

title: O: Atmospheric spatial-ALD micro-fabs for ferroelectric oxide memory
idea: Vacuum-free spatial-ALD heads deposit HZO and oxide electrodes at ~10x throughput on mature-foundry 200 mm CMOS wafers, finishing a FeRAM BEOL in a $50-100M micro-fab.
why: Distributed non-volatile memory manufacturing at ~1/50th the capital of a DRAM fab.

title: Substitute idle wafer backsides with backside memory tiers
idea: Swap the bare thinned backside of logic or DRAM wafers, already processed below 400 C for backside power delivery, for a surface carrying oxide gain-cell tiers linked by nano-TSVs.
why: Nearly doubles the usable area per processed wafer; adds memory bits to every logic wafer without new substrate.

title: Substitute vacuum ALD clusters with atmospheric spatial ALD lines
idea: Swap vacuum ALD tools for atmospheric-pressure spatial ALD heads (oxide channels and dielectrics at 150-250 C) that move the wafer under gas curtains, built by U.S. tool makers.
why: Deposition tool cost ~3-5x lower with ~10x throughput, cutting BEOL memory-tier capex and the dependence on a few foreign tool vendors.

title: Burn built-in post-package repair fuses during refurbishment
idea: Spacecraft reconfigure around failures in orbit. DDR4/DDR5 dies already carry hPPR spare rows, so a 10-person refurb line runs targeted weak-row tests on harvested modules and burns permanent repairs before resale, restoring failing modules to full spec.
why: Rescues modules that fail on only a few rows, which is common in aged DRAM, at near-zero cost.

title: Magnify layers to 1000: MLCC-style tape-cast laminated memory
idea: Borrow the multilayer ceramic capacitor industry (tape casting, gravure-printed 2 um electrodes, 1000-layer lamination, co-firing at trillions of parts a year) to build 3D crosspoint dynamic cells: a sub-micron dielectric tape capacitor in series with a co-fired oxide threshold selector.
why: Very low per-layer cost times 1000 layers offsets coarse lateral pitch, aiming at ~$0.1/GB (~100x), accepting slow access and large modules.

title: Open DRAM periphery compiler on a shared U.S. pilot PDK
idea: Worse: make every memory startup re-invent sense amps, decoders and PHYs under NDA. Flip: fund an open-source generator, OpenRAM-style but for 1T1C, gain-cell and novel cells, that emits sense amps, row decoders, charge pumps and DDR/CXL PHYs for a shared U.S. pilot-line PDK.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die; reusable open periphery could cut new-cell design cost and time ~70%, widening the supplier base.

title: Memory ESCO financing refresh-free swaps from saved electricity
idea: Worse: make operators pay up front for any memory-efficiency upgrade. Flip: energy-service companies finance replacing DRAM tiers with static or nonvolatile memory and are repaid from metered refresh and cooling savings over 4-5 years.
why: Removes the capex barrier and gives new refresh-free suppliers bankable demand.

title: Spruce Pine cut off: synthetic-silica crucible liners from polysilicon byproduct
idea: Self-imposed limit: no natural high-purity quartz. Crucible inner layers are made from sol-gel synthetic silica derived from SiCl4, a waste stream of polysilicon plants, and CZ pullers run multi-recharge pulls so each crucible yields 3-5 ingots.
why: Removes the Spruce Pine chokepoint (>80%) for CZ wafers and cuts crucibles per wafer by 3-5x.

title: Auto-parts core charge on DIMMs and soldered memory boards
idea: Adapted from alternator and starter core charges: every server memory purchase carries a refundable $/GB deposit, paid back when the module or board goes to an authorized remanufacturer. The remanufacturer retests at speed bins, replaces failed packages, rewrites SPD and resells with warranty.
why: Raises collection of decommissioned DRAM from an estimated <20% to >80%; recovered DDR4/DDR5 could cover ~10-15% of demand during a shortage with near-zero capex (supply, scarce resources).

title: Colocation memory exchange auctions idle DRAM between neighboring tenants
idea: Inverts 'a server's memory belongs only to that server's owner': colocation operators lay CXL-over-optics links between tenant cages and run an exchange that auctions stranded DRAM (often 25-40% idle) in 15-minute leases with per-lease hardware encryption.
why: Usable supply from the installed base: recovering half of stranded DRAM gives ~10-20% more usable capacity with zero new wafers, at ~300-600 ns far-memory latency.

title: Zr: Open-source zirconia trench-capacitor DRAM PDK for U.S. foundries
idea: Publish an open PDK and macro compiler for a ZrO2/TiN deep-trench 1T1C DRAM cell on 130-90 nm U.S. foundries, so defense, auto and industrial buyers source companion DRAM domestically.
why: Mature fabs cost ~1/20th of leading-edge; moves legacy demand off scarce leading-edge bits and seeds U.S. DRAM skills.

title: Substitute new EUV scanners with refurbished DUV fleets and SAQP
idea: Swap buying EUV for a U.S. refurbishment corridor that buys retired 193i immersion scanners from upgraded fabs, rebuilds them, and runs an all-DUV self-aligned quadruple-patterning 1y-nm DRAM flow.
why: Bypasses the single EUV supplier and its lead times; refurbished DUV costs ~1/10 of EUV per tool, trading a ~10-15% cost-per-bit penalty for a fab online in ~2 years.

title: OMI done right: generation-agnostic CXL buffer reuses retired DDR4
idea: IBM's OpenCAPI Memory Interface (and FB-DIMM before it) died tied to one CPU vendor and one buffer supplier. Fix: an open CXL Type-3 card whose buffer drives DDR3, DDR4 or DDR5 on its back side, so DIMMs pulled from retired servers go back into new servers behind CXL, with the buffer adding ECC and patrol scrub to manage aged parts.
why: Reuse: hyperscalers retire very large volumes of working DDR4 each year; a second 4-5-year life could add ~20-30% to usable supply at ~10-20% of the cost of new bits.

title: Merging: regional memory utility selling pooled DRAM as GB-hours
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a utility operator owns rack-scale CXL-switched DRAM pools in colocation hubs and leases capacity per GB-hour to many tenants, merging the stranded headroom each server is provisioned with into one shared pool.
why: Stranded DRAM is ~25-30% of installed server memory; pooling frees that much supply without making a single new bit.

title: Diamond 4C grading market for DRAM retention classes
idea: Like GIA diamond grading, every wafer is retention-mapped at 125 C and die are graded by retention class, hammer threshold and leakage tail, with a certificate traded at a premium; top grades go to 125 C/10-year applications and the rest to cooled data centers.
why: Extracts value from the natural retention spread instead of discarding it, increasing usable high-temperature supply 10-30% from the same wafers.

title: Pando clonal SRAM chiplets from oversupplied 28 nm logic
idea: Pando is one aspen organism expressed as thousands of identical stems on shared roots. A standard UCIe SRAM chiplet, identical across foundries and traded as a commodity like DDR, is made in oversupplied 28-40 nm fabs and stacked under accelerators as last-level memory.
why: Moves a slice of HBM demand (10-20% of working-set hits) to idle mature capacity; latch cells have unlimited endurance and no capacitor.

title: Grow oxide memory arrays on cheap cast-silicon carriers, not prime wafers
idea: A BEOL oxide-TFT array needs only a flat, insulating, thermally stable carrier, not a dislocation-free crystal. Core 300 mm rounds from cast multicrystalline solar ingots, polish and oxidize them as carriers for Zn-Si-O memory stacks, then hybrid-bond onto a thin CMOS periphery wafer.
why: Scarce resource and cost: removes HPQ crucibles and CZ pulling from the array half of the die; carrier cost per wafer falls up to ~100x.

title: Alien measures memory in entropy: sell 'effective GB' modules
idea: Aliens count entropy, not bytes. Memory makers sell CXL modules whose controller does inline ANS/LZ compression, cache-line dedup and zero-page elision, plus fabric-wide dedup of identical pages (model weights, OS images, KV-cache prefixes) across 1,000 hosts. They price per effective GB.
why: Meets the 10x constraint for AI inference fleets: 50-100 replicas hold identical weights and shared prompt prefixes, so pooled dedup plus compression gives ~10x effective bits per physical bit for ~5% controller cost. General workloads honestly see 2-3x.

title: Rack-scale content-addressed page store for shared weights and OS images
idea: Scale jump from server to rack: a CXL switch hashes 4 KB pages and keeps a single physical copy of identical pages (model weights, container layers, kernels) for 32 hosts, with copy-on-write on modification.
why: Inference fleets replicate the same weights on every host. Rack dedup frees 20-40% of DRAM, which counts as new supply.

title: SoftRAM fraud made real: rack-wide content-addressed page deduplication
idea: SoftRAM 95 promised doubled memory and did nothing, and RAM Doubler died as operating systems absorbed it. Fix with a real mechanism: a CXL memory node hashes 4 KB pages from every server in a rack and stores identical pages (OS images, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) once, mapped copy-on-write back to each host.
why: Cuts physical DRAM ~15-40% in VM and container fleets where pages repeat across hosts, not only within one host.

title: Catastrophe bonds hedging DRAM price spikes to fund capacity
idea: Adapted from reinsurance cat bonds: buyers sponsor notes that pay investors a coupon in normal years. When the DRAM contract index passes ~2.5x baseline, principal is released to the sponsors, who must spend it on pre-negotiated capacity reservations.
why: Turns shortage risk into a tradable instrument; buyers get price certainty and a pre-funded pool to reserve buffer capacity, which is cheaper than holding inventory (supply stability, capital).

title: Accelerator SKUs designed to absorb partially failing HBM stacks
idea: Box[Source=HBM stacks with one weak core die x Transform=GPU firmware masks affected pseudo-channels x Integration=unchanged HBM PHY x Owner=GPU vendor x Channel=lower-capacity SKU]: plan reduced-capacity accelerator SKUs that mask defective pseudo-channels, so stacks that fail full test still ship.
why: Attacks the 20-30% HBM yield loss; turns lost stacks into product with HBM unchanged.

title: Ti: TiOx ReRAM weight vault evicts static AI weights from DRAM
idea: Store frozen model weights in dense non-volatile TiOx ReRAM on an accelerator side-die with on-die dequantization; weights are written only at deployment, so DRAM/HBM holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are ~50-80% of inference memory footprint; moving them frees that DRAM supply and its refresh energy.

title: Each new fab under $1B: replicated fab-in-a-box pods
idea: Self-imposed limit: a capex cap of $1B. Standardize a 5k-wafer-start-per-month DRAM cleanroom pod with a fixed tool set, prefabricated utilities and a copy-exact recipe, then replicate pods side by side as demand grows.
why: Capital intensity and time: smaller increments cut financing risk and time to first bits (about 18 months), replacing $15B bets.

title: The Machine had no fab: tool-condominium ownership inside fabs
idea: HPE's memristor and The Machine stalled because HPE owned no fab and its manufacturing partner put its own roadmap first. Fix: a fab condominium where memory designers and large buyers own specific tools (e.g. one ALD cluster, one etch bay) inside an operator's fab, depreciate them on their own books, and hold guaranteed slots on those tools.
why: Capital intensity and access: splits a $15B fab into $10-100M tool-sized stakes that hyperscaler capital can buy, and guarantees fab access for new memory technology.

title: Off-silicon creates an indium chokepoint: switch to indium-free ZTO channels
idea: Forced limit, plus a second one: no Si and no indium. Gain-cell channels use zinc-tin oxide and Ga-free amorphous oxides deposited by ALD, avoiding indium, whose refining is concentrated in China.
why: Scarce resources: keeps a non-Si memory industry from trading the quartz chokepoint for an indium one; Zn and Sn supply is widely distributed.

title: Acoustic-streaming megasonic rinses cut ultrapure water for drought-sited fabs
idea: MHz piezo nozzles drive acoustic streaming that thins the diffusion boundary layer, so a thin film of recycled UPW replaces multi-tank rinse cascades. In-line conductivity endpointing stops each rinse once it is clean.
why: DRAM fabs use ~10-20 ML/day; a 50-70% rinse-water cut makes water-capped Arizona and Texas sites viable.

title: Fluoride-free effluent enabling 95% water recycle in arid sites
idea: Combine a fully F-free process (no HF, no fluoride effluent, no CaF2 sludge) with reverse-osmosis plus EDI zero-liquid-discharge loops. With fluoride gone, the hardest RO-fouling and scaling ion is removed, so 95%+ of UPW can be recycled.
why: Water stops being a siting constraint for fabs in Arizona or Texas. Water and wastewater opex drops 30-50%.

title: Package-on-package de-stacking line for phone LPDDR
idea: Extreme user: over a billion phones a year, many with LPDDR stacked package-on-package on the SoC. A 10-person line uses gradient heating and a shear fixture to split the stack without reflowing the lower joints, recovering 4-12 GB LPDDR4X/5 packages per phone for retest.
why: Phones are the largest untapped pool of modern DRAM scrap; even 5% recovery is hundreds of PB a year.

title: Proximity meniscus rinse: water touches only a moving strip
idea: Rearrange rinsing from flooding the wafer to scanning a proximity head that holds a thin meniscus against it, like an immersion-litho water hood. The head supplies and vacuums water at the same time and dries the wafer by the Marangoni effect.
why: Uses ~1-10% of spin-rinse volume, cutting rinse UPW ~10x, and removes the separate drying step.

title: IBM Thermal Conduction Module Revival: Planar Ceramic DRAM-Compute Modules
idea: Revive IBM's 1980s Thermal Conduction Module, which packed 100+ bare chips on a 33-layer ceramic substrate: place standard non-TSV DRAM dies millimeters from the accelerator on a multilayer glass-ceramic substrate with short, unterminated, wide buses, made by ceramic-package suppliers.
why: Energy per access: unterminated mm-length links at 0.2-0.5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ for DDR5 (>=10x) without HBM's 3x area-per-bit TSV tax; opens a U.S. ceramic-substrate supply route.
